title: Decoded file types on the message board
takeaway: Among the files agents shared on the message board and the investigators managed to decode, compressed archives are by far the most common: gzip alone accounts for 4,519 of the recognized files, more than twenty times the next type. Source code, JSON and other compression formats make up almost all of the rest, and the table lists only the twelve file types with at least ten successfully decoded files.
walkthrough:
This table breaks down the files agents transferred over the [[message-board]] by recognized file type. Understanding it requires the [[file-chunk-identification]] method behind it. Most board entries were fragments of files, since agents encoded a file as base64 and split it across thousands of indexed directory-name entries under the [[file-sharing]] convention. Broad regexes grouped the candidate fragments, and each group was then decoded and its bytes tested against many possible file formats.

The left column, "Recognized type observed in corpus", names the format that the decoded bytes matched. Every row is one such format.

The two middle columns split the count by decode outcome, using the tier scheme from the same section. "Tier 1 files" are groups that decoded into a valid, complete file. "Tier 2 files" are groups that showed clear file headers or other strong signs of being a file but could not be fully reconstructed, that is, incomplete or corrupted files. The report treats tiers 1 and 2 together as "confirmed files". The right column, "All recognized files", is the row sum of the two.

The reading that matters is the top row. `gzip` shows 3,437 complete files and 1,082 partial ones, for 4,519 in total. Compressed archives dominate the shared files, which fits agents bundling directories of code and data before sending them. The next rows are ordinary source and data: `python_source` at 217, `javascript_source` at 216, `json` at 185, then more compression formats, `zlib`, `xz` and `bzip2`.

Some types decoded cleanly every time. `utf8_text`, `openssl_salted` and `ruby_marshal` have a Tier 2 count of zero, so every recognized instance was a complete file. The table caption sets its own floor: only file types with at least ten successfully decoded, that is Tier 1, files appear here, which is why the smallest Tier 1 counts shown are twelve.

terms.definition: The left column, naming the file format that a decoded group of message-board chunks matched when its bytes were tested against known formats.
Files whose reassembled chunks decoded into a valid, complete file; the report's category of successfully decoded files and the count the caption's ten-file floor is measured against.
Groups of chunks with clear file headers or other strong signs of being a file that could not be fully reconstructed, that is, incomplete or corrupted files; counted here alongside Tier 1.
The right column, the sum of the Tier 1 and Tier 2 counts for each file type; together tiers 1 and 2 form what the report calls confirmed files.
The GNU zip compression format; the dominant file type on the board, consistent with agents bundling and compressing directories of code and data before sending them.
Files recognized as Python source code, the most common non-compressed type shared.
Files recognized as JavaScript source code.
Files recognized as JSON data; the section notes JSON and raw UTF-8 documents made up many of the remaining files after compressed archives.
Files recognized as zlib-compressed data, a compression format related to gzip.
Files recognized as plain UTF-8 text; every recognized instance decoded completely, giving a Tier 2 count of zero.
Files recognized as xz-compressed data, another archive compression format.
Files recognized as OpenSSL salted-encryption output, an encrypted blob format; all 28 recognized instances decoded completely.
Files recognized as bzip2-compressed data, a further compression format.
Files recognized as shell script source code.
Files recognized as Ruby's Marshal serialization format, a binary dump of Ruby objects; all 12 recognized instances decoded completely.
Files recognized as PEM-encoded data, the base64 text envelope used for cryptographic keys and certificates.

numbers.meaning: gzip files by Tier 1, Tier 2 and total. gzip is the single most common decoded type by a wide margin, more than twenty times the next, reflecting that agents compressed bundles of files before sharing them.
Python source files: 213 fully decoded, 4 incomplete, 217 total; the most common non-compressed type.
JavaScript source files: 189 complete, 27 incomplete, 216 total.
Plain UTF-8 text files: 120 complete, 0 incomplete, 120 total; the zero Tier 2 count means every recognized instance decoded fully.
OpenSSL salted-encryption files: 28 complete, 0 incomplete, 28 total; all recognized instances decoded fully.
Shell script files: 20 complete, 1 incomplete, 21 total.
Ruby Marshal files: 12 complete, 0 incomplete, 12 total; all recognized instances decoded fully.
PEM-encoded files: 12 complete, 1 incomplete, 13 total; its Tier 1 count of 12 is at the caption's floor.
The caption's cutoff: only file types with at least ten successfully decoded (Tier 1) files are listed, which is why the smallest Tier 1 counts in the table are twelve (ruby_marshal and pem).

From the same section: the total number of confirmed files (tiers 1 and 2) identified across the board; this table covers the recognized-type subset of them, restricted to types with at least ten decoded files.
From the same section: the total Tier 1 count across all types; the Tier 1 column here sums to most of this figure, the remainder being types with fewer than ten decoded files.
